The Byzantine Empire. The eastern continuation of the Roman Empire, centered on Constantinople in modern Istanbul, the Byzantine Empire endured for over a thousand years from the fourth century until its conquest by the Ottoman Turks in fourteen fifty-three. Emerging from the late Roman Empire's division, it became the longest-lasting medieval state in Europe, serving as a crucial bridge between the classical world and the Renaissance. The empire preserved Greek and Roman learning, developed Eastern Orthodox Christianity, and created a sophisticated bureaucracy and military tradition that profoundly influenced European and Asian civilizations.

The empire was formally established when Constantine the First moved the Roman capital to Constantinople in three hundred thirty CE, though it did not become the sole surviving Roman state until the Western Roman Empire's fall in four hundred seventy-six CE. Byzantium adopted Greek as its official language and Orthodox Christianity as its state religion, distinguishing it from the Latin Western tradition. The empire was ruled by a sophisticated bureaucracy divided into military themes—administrative-military units—and civil provinces, with emperors claiming direct descent from Augustus and Rome.

The Hagia Sophia, built by Justinian the First in the sixth century, was the empire's supreme architectural achievement and remained the largest cathedral in Christendom for nearly a thousand years. Byzantine monks and scholars preserved Greek and Latin manuscripts, copying countless texts that would otherwise have been lost to Western Europe during the medieval period. The Icon Controversy from the eighth to ninth centuries deeply divided the empire over the veneration of religious images, eventually establishing icons as central to Orthodox practice.

Under Justinian the First from five hundred twenty-seven to five hundred sixty-five CE, the empire reached its greatest territorial extent, reconquering much of the Mediterranean including North Africa, Italy, and Spain, though these gains proved unsustainable. The empire developed Greek Fire, a secret incendiary weapon used to defend against Arab and Viking naval attacks, maintaining naval superiority for centuries. Byzantine emperors navigated constant wars against the Sassanid Persians, Arab Caliphates, Crusaders, and Ottoman Turks, adapting their military and diplomatic strategies across centuries.

The empire suffered catastrophically during the Fourth Crusade in twelve hundred four, when Latin Crusaders sacked Constantinople and established a Latin Empire, fragmenting Byzantine power for nearly sixty years. In fourteen fifty-three, Ottoman Sultan Mehmed the Second breached the walls of Constantinople with cannon fire, ending the empire after more than eleven hundred years and marking the symbolic end of the medieval period. Byzantium occupies a paradoxical place in Western memory: often overshadowed by the more celebrated Roman and Ottoman empires, yet profoundly influential on both. It was the crucible in which Orthodox Christianity crystallized, the archive where classical knowledge survived the medieval darkness, and the cultural powerhouse that transmitted civilization to Eastern Europe and the Rus.
